item.title: When Holidays Amplify Teen Anxiety
item.description:
Holidays are supposed to be exciting and magical. At least that is what every story wants us to believe through all of its decorated windows and social media feeds. Every family tradition tells us that we need to have all the things so we can have the best of times during the most wonderful time of the year. But for many teens, there is nothing magical about the season. Beyond the bright lights and family dinner, teens find themselves struggling with anxiety.

They are caught between the feelings that everyone says they must have and what they actually experience. It is a contradiction that runs deeper than family members realize. Teens are behind the scenes, trying to navigate a stage in life where they are already questioning more than just the holiday feelings. Most teens deal with these questions on a daily basis:

  • Who am I?
  • Where do I fit in?
  • What am I here for?

The holidays tend to intensify these questions and create a spotlight on family dynamics. Social connections and personal worth come to the forefront of the season, and teens have a hard time knowing how to react to the scrutiny. Still, we are reminded of hope for anxiety in the Scriptures:

Do not be anxious about anything, but in every situation, by prayer and petition, with thanksgiving, present your requests to God. And the peace of God, which transcends all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus. – Philippians 4:6-7, NIV

The Weight of Holiday Expectations and Teen Anxiety

There is an unspoken rule in most households during the holidays. The one that says everyone must be happy, grateful, and full of holiday cheer. For most teenagers, it can be challenging to incorporate this into the already complex ideologies they navigate daily. They look at their surroundings to find scenes of curated social media posts that show nothing but perfect family moments.

The reality behind the photos seen in social media feeds does not show the arguments and forced smiles that led up to the photos. Teens find themselves exhausted from pretending everything is wonderful and perfect. As they scroll, teens see the polished version and feel that they have issues because their feelings do not match the scene captured for the sake of getting likes on a post. This gap feeds anxiety that is often difficult to name.

The cultural message says they must be authentic and, at the same time, demands they express happiness. The unspoken message is to be yourself, but be sure it is cheerful and low-maintenance.

They can express their feelings only if those feelings do not disrupt the holiday spirit. These harsh contradictions create an internal pressure cooker. Christian counselors often see teens during January who spent December falling apart behind a mask of holiday compliance.

When Family Gatherings Become a Stage

Extended family gatherings often carry their own unique stress. Family members they hardly see are barraging them with questions that feel like an evaluation. They feel as though they are being tested and could be failing. The noise of overlapping conversations and the constant pressure to smile make it even harder to relax.

This anxiety comes from being seen as something other than a person. Relatives offer well-meaning advice about everything from life choices to appearance. This brings a new weight of judgment, even though it’s hidden in the holiday sparkle. Teens may become hyper-fixated on wondering who is watching them and how they are being assessed. To them, every interaction becomes a performance, and they must represent the family while being themselves.

During these holiday gatherings, some teens retreat into silence while others overcompensate with forced enthusiasm. Either way, teens are not truly present. They’re managing anxiety at the same time they are trying to meet expectations that feel impossible to satisfy.

The holidays become less about connection and more about survival. Just getting through each gathering without disappointing anyone or revealing how much they struggle becomes the unintended goal.

The Isolation that Comes with Holiday Breaks

The strange paradox of holiday breaks is that teens are surrounded by family, yet they feel utterly alone. The daily structure that normally holds your anxiety at bay disappears. There’s no school schedule, no regular friend interactions, and no routine to distract them from the anxious thoughts that typically run rampant. This sudden emptiness creates a space for worry to expand and take over.

Teens typically push anxiety off to the side between classes and activities during the school year. However, extended time at home removes those barriers, and hours will leave them with nothing but their own thoughts. Social media may show friends traveling or celebrating, which intensifies feelings of isolation. They are physically present with the family, but they are emotionally disconnected, and nobody around them seems to understand they are experiencing this.

This isolation will feed on itself, and the teen will withdraw because they don’t want to burden their families with their struggles. This leads families to believe everything is fine because the teen is at home and seems relaxed. The gap between internal experience and external perception widens. Christian counselors recognize this pattern, and they realize the holiday season often brings a spike in teen anxiety that goes unnoticed until it reaches a point of crisis.

Finding Solid Ground When Everything Feels Uncertain

Faith can offer the consistency the holiday season lacks. It has a foundation that doesn’t shift based on circumstances or expectations. Connecting with God will provide an anchor when everything else feels unstable for teens who struggle with anxiety. This isn’t about having a perfect faith or acting as though anxiety doesn’t exist. It is about bringing the mess and confusion to someone who can handle it and provide peace in the chaos.

One avenue for teens to release anxiety is prayer. Prayer is about having an all-encompassing conversation with God and not trying to find formal words just to seem spiritual. The fear, the feelings of being overwhelmed, and the confusion about why they are struggling with happiness can be the basis of telling God exactly how they feel.

Journaling prayers can be helpful when anxiety makes it hard to have cohesive thoughts. Writing out the worries and leaving them on a page can imitate a tangible release of those worries.

There are no generic platitudes in the Scriptures that offer specific promises for anxious moments. God’s word is an assurance that he understands those moments, and he doesn’t leave them alone to navigate their feelings. By memorizing Scripture, teens can get something solid to hold onto when panic rises.

Christian counselors work with teens to cultivate spiritual practices that will feel authentic and not performative. Small rhythms will create a space for peace rather than add to the holiday obligations.

Community can play a big part in helping teens navigate anxiety during the holidays. Finding other teens to understand the struggle will break the isolation. Youth groups and faith-based support systems provide all spaces where teens can drop the performance and just experience the reality of life.

These are spaces where they can admit that the holidays are hard without being told they’re ungrateful. Sometimes just knowing others share similar experiences lessens the grip of anxiety. Instead, they can experience the peace described in John:

Peace I leave with you; my peace I give you. I do not give to you as the world gives. Do not let your hearts be troubled and do not be afraid. – John 14:27, NIV

Support for Teens with Anxiety During the Holidays

The holidays can be inherently complex for teens, and this is a reality to accept rather than fix. Recognizing this truth allows for genuine healing. Pretending everything should be joyful is unrealistic, and teens need adults who can support them through difficult times without rushing to fix things.

It’s important to validate that while the season is challenging, they are not broken or ungrateful. Amid holiday anxiety, there is hope. It is not the superficial kind, but a deeper hope rooted in the belief that God is present in the chaos. Faith doesn’t mean having everything together, and seeking help from Christian counselors or trusted adults is a sign of wisdom.

item.title: Managing Anger Outbursts: A Faith-Based Approach for Work Leaders
item.description:
Leadership in the workplace comes with unique pressures, including deadlines to meet, teams to motivate, conflicts to resolve, and performance standards to maintain. The combination of all these demands can build up until it overflows in surprising ways. Anger outbursts don’t just disrupt the workday; they also disrupt the workplace. They reveal something deeper about how we manage stress, set boundaries, and acknowledge limitations.

For Christian leaders, these moments can feel like a failure of faith as losing composure means losing ground spiritually. The reality is that, beyond the surface, we carry unprocessed emotions and needs that support both honoring our humanity and our faith.

In your anger do not sin: Do not let the sun go down while you are still angry. – Ephesians 4:26, NIV

The Weight of Leadership Expectations

In today’s workplace, leaders navigate impossible standards. They are expected to be decisive but collaborative, strong yet empathetic, and results-driven yet people-focused. All of these dual expectations have created an environment where stress accumulates without adequate release.

Anger in the workplace often stems from chronic pressure that has not been addressed, rather than a single incident. Leaders face the additional burden of maintaining composure, while others could express frustration more freely. The result is an imbalance that builds internal pressure, which eventually erupts.

When faith enters the picture, the challenge of an anger outburst deepens. Christian leaders emphasize that anger itself is sinful, which leads to shame if they exhibit an outburst. However, Scripture acknowledges anger as part of the human experience. The issue comes with what we do with that anger.

We either let anger control us or bring it before God and seek a healthy way to process it. Christian counselors understand the challenge and help leaders develop strategies that are both emotionally healthy and promote spiritual growth.

Recognizing the Triggers Behind Anger Outbursts

Anger outbursts at work rarely happen without warning. There are patterns these outbursts follow that we can identify when we’re paying attention. Common triggers include feeling disrespected, experiencing a loss of control, facing repeated obstacles, or dealing with a perceived injustice.

For many leaders, the most common triggers involve team members failing to meet expectations, upper management imposing unrealistic demands, and feeling caught between conflicting priorities. To understand your specific triggers, you must engage in honest self-reflection about the situations that consistently elevate your stress.

This process requires you to examine the interactions that leave you feeling defensive, dismissed, or tense in your body. The physical symptoms in your body often precede the outburst, offering a window for intervention. Keeping a log of anger episodes can reveal patterns that might otherwise go unnoticed. You may find common themes that point to underlying issues that need to be addressed.

Throughout Scripture, we are encouraged to be wise in our anger. Proverbs is full of clear directives like this:

The one who has knowledge uses words with restraint, and whoever has understanding is even-tempered. – Proverbs 17:27, NIV

The Impact on Teams and Trust

The effects of anger outbursts ripple throughout the organization. Team members become cautious and second-guess their decisions to avoid risks. Communication suffers as people withhold information that may trigger a negative response. Creativity dwindles when the environment feels unpredictable or unsafe.

The paradox is that leaders who struggle with anger care deeply about their teams and their work. The outburst comes from investment, not indifference, but the impact remains the same regardless of intent.

To rebuild trust after an outburst will require more than a simple apology. Acknowledging the harm that was caused and taking responsibility without justification is the first step toward demonstrating changed behavior.

This reflects the heart of Christian leadership: modeling, humility, repentance, and growth, in a way that inspires teams to respect leaders who own their mistakes and actively work toward change. Authenticity will strengthen relationships more than maintaining the façade of perfection.

Leaders can find support from Christian counselors as they navigate the restoration process, with practical steps and spiritual grounding. They will be given tools for repairing relationships while addressing the root causes of the outburst. The dual focus will prevent the cycle from repeating while healing the present damage.

Developing Healthy Anger Management Strategies

There is a combination of immediate techniques and long-term lifestyle changes required to manage anger effectively. In the moment of anger, a simple practice can interrupt the anger response before it escalates, which includes taking a brief pause before responding. Excusing yourself from the situation or using deep breathing won’t suppress the anger, but it will create space between the trigger and your response.

Long-term strategies address conditions that make an outburst more likely. Reducing overall stress levels and providing a healthy outlet for intense emotions can be done through regular exercise, nutrition, and consistent hydration, which also affects emotional regulation.

It is also important to understand how to set realistic boundaries at work. Saying no to additional projects, delegating effectively, and taking breaks during the day will prevent the accumulation of pressure that can lead to explosions.

Christian leaders can be grounded through prayer and Scripture reading that counters the false narrative anger creates. When you get angry, you tend to catastrophize, personalize, and assume the worst. God’s word offers a different perspective, reminding us of our identity in Christ rather than our performance at work. Spiritual practices will complement professional support and address the practical and internal dimensions of our struggles.

My dear brothers and sisters, take note of this: Everyone should be quick to listen, slow to speak, and slow to become angry. – James 1:19, NIV

When to Seek Professional Support

There are times when self-help strategies aren’t enough to help with anger outbursts that are increasing in frequency or intensity. When you feel out of control during episodes or when you’re using substances to manage emotions, professional support is likely needed. This is not an indication of weakness, but rather a reflection of Christian wisdom. Christian counselors can offer specialized help that integrates mental health expertise with biblical truth.

Counseling will provide a confidential and safe space to explore the deeper issues beneath the anger, such as unresolved trauma, chronic stress, identity confusion, or other spiritual struggles. Many leaders identify that anger is a secondary emotion that masks fear, grief, or shame. When these are addressed, the entire dynamic of the workplace changes.

Counselors can also help with advanced anger management techniques that are tailored to your specific situation. This will help cultivate a personalized plan that fits your faith and your life.

When you reach out for help, it often reflects a turning point and demonstrates the strength to admit that you need support and the courage to pursue growth. This reflects trust in God’s provision through professional support that he makes available. The journey to healing leads to freedom, even when it’s not always comfortable. This freedom allows clarity, responds with grace, and models the transformation that faith makes possible.

A Plan for Managing Anger Outbursts

Anger outbursts do not define you as a leader, but they do reveal areas where growth is needed. The pressure, expectations, and demands of work are real, and the emotional toll is significant. These challenges come with opportunities to develop greater self-awareness, healthier coping strategies, and a deeper dependence on God.

When you manage anger well, it doesn’t mean you won’t feel it. It means you will acknowledge it, honestly understand what triggers it, and choose to respond in a way that aligns with your faith. The process will take time, support, and grace from God and yourself.

Transformation happens gradually. Remember: small steps consistently taken produce lasting change. Counseling, spiritual practice, lifestyle adjustment, or a combination of these can cultivate a path toward healthier anger management. This journey does not have to be navigated alone, and you do not have to remain stuck in patterns that harm yourself or others.

item.title: How to Find the Best Therapist for Your Needs
item.description:
Choosing a therapist is personal, and it may take a little work to find the one who is the best fit for you, especially if this is a first-time experience, you’re not sure where to start, and you have no sense of what to look for.

This article on how to find the best therapist aims at providing you with the basic information and practical suggestions you need to help point you in the right direction so that you know what to look for and guide you through the selection process.

Important Issues to Consider Before You Begin Your Search

As you search for how to find the best therapist, it is helpful to have an idea of what you are looking for. Maybe you need help managing a specific issue, such as depression or anxiety, improving the way you communicate with others, or working through the effects of a traumatic experience.

Perhaps you don’t have a clear-cut goal but would just like to feel better, learn some practical tools for coping with and navigating stressful situations, or simply have a safe space where you can talk openly about your issues without feeling judged.

Other important issues include verifying credentials, checking insurance coverage, and demographic preferences. Will therapy be covered by insurance, for instance, or will you need to pay out of pocket? Or would you be more comfortable seeing someone of a specific gender, age, race, religious affiliation, culture, or background?

Types of Therapists

Therapists have a range of degrees and titles that indicate their different levels of education and training, and the letters after their names can be confusing.

Psychologists (PhD/PsyD), for instance, are mental health professionals with doctorate degrees who are qualified to diagnose and treat mental health conditions.

Licensed Clinical Social Workers (LCSWs) hold a master’s degree or higher, can diagnose and treat mental health conditions, and are also able to connect you to resources in your community.

Licensed Professional Counselors or Therapists (LPC/LCPC/LMHC) have a master’s degree or higher and can diagnose and treat mental health disorders.

Licensed Marriage and Family Therapists (LMFTs) specialize in issues relating to couples, families, and relationships.

Although studies have shown that a therapist’s specific degree or the letters following their name may not be as important as their approach to therapy and your connection with them, you need to make sure that they are licensed mental health professionals who have met licensing qualifications.

Determine whether they have an advanced degree, passed a licensing test and background check, follow specific guidelines and ethical codes, and that they have the right specialization and experience to treat your issue.

If your insurance covers the cost of therapy, your therapist also needs to be licensed to practice in your state.

Types of Therapy Therapists Provide

Therapists use different approaches to help you work through your challenges. Some approaches, for instance, focus on thoughts and behaviors, help you identify maladaptive patterns in your thinking, and learn to identify and reframe them.

Other approaches may focus on emotions, relationships, and past experiences, and how early childhood wounds may still be shaping your reactions today. Some examples include:

Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) CBT focuses on helping you recognize and reframe maladaptive thought patterns and behaviors.

Dialectical Behavioral Therapy (DBT) DBT helps you learn how to regulate your emotions and improve your relationships, and equips you with practical techniques for coping with difficult situations.

Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) Acceptance and commitment therapy focuses on the here and now and teaches you to acknowledge and accept your emotions and feelings without judging them, rather than trying to control or fix them.

Psychodynamic Therapy Psychodynamic therapy focuses on past influences and helps you gain insight into how early childhood experiences may subconsciously affect your present behavior, feelings, and relationships.

Starting Your Search

A good place to begin your search is by asking for recommendations and checking online directories and resources such as Google or Yelp, which typically provide detailed profiles including credentials, specialties, insurances the therapists accept, location, and availability, as well as reviews and testimonials that can offer insight into their approaches and success rate.

Make a list of possible candidates and then narrow it down by visiting the websites and social media pages of the therapists on your list, where you can read their bios and posts, and get a better sense of their communication style, personality, and who they are.

After you have done your research and narrowed down your list of possible candidates, reach out to them by e-mail or a phone call to introduce yourself, tell them what your concerns are and why you are seeking therapy, what you are hoping to achieve, why you think they may be a good fit, and ask them what their availability is.

Use their responses to further narrow down your list according to whether or not they have openings, are in an easily accessible location, take your insurance, are able to work with your schedule, have an understanding of the area you want to work on, and are able to help you with the issues you need help with.

Pick three to five you have the best feelings about and set up an appointment for a short consultation, either in person or over the phone, so you can ask questions, gauge your comfort level with them, and assess how well you connect.

Examples of questions to ask during this initial interview include:

  • How much experience they have had working with others who have your specific type of challenge.
  • How long sessions last and how often per week they would want to see you.
  • Whether they conduct virtual as well as in-person sessions.
  • Whether they use a blended approach or stick strictly to one specific method.
  • How much they charge per session and whether they have a sliding scale according to income if you don’t have insurance, or are willing to set up a payment plan.
  • If there is a fee for missed or canceled sessions.
  • Whether they accept texts or phone calls.
  • And how long they anticipate therapy for your issue to take – would it be short-term or long-term.

Therapy is a relationship with another person. Rapport is important. You don’t just want someone with the right degree or price range, but rather, someone you feel comfortable with, who gets you, and whose style aligns with your needs.

You’ll know when you have found the right therapist for you when you feel safe, supported, and motivated when you meet with them.

Signs of a Good Therapist

Studies indicate that the number one predictor of successful therapy is not training, years of experience, or the type of therapy itself, but rather, your relationship with your therapist. It’s having an empathetic connection with him or her that enables you to feel safe opening up and allowing yourself to be vulnerable.

Although having more experience and training may be helpful, in the end, what makes a therapist great are personality factors such as compassion, insightfulness, and understanding.

In addition to being knowledgeable about your specific issues, a good therapist is genuine, totally present with you, able to tune into what you are feeling, comprehend the struggles you are describing, interpret the thoughts and feelings you express, and put them into words for you, and is someone who validates you and respects your point of view.

In-Person Versus Virtual Therapy

Both in-person and virtual therapy can be equally effective. The right choice is a matter of what you feel most comfortable with.

Benefits of in-person therapy include meeting face-to-face with someone in a dedicated space and being able to pick up on subtle nonverbal cues.

Virtual therapy, on the other hand, makes therapy more easily accessible as you are not limited by location. It can also be more convenient, save time, and be of special benefit to people with busy schedules, limited local options, transportation challenges, or who may be homebound.

Secular Versus Christian Therapy

Some believers are under the false impression that seeking therapy is unbiblical or indicates a lack of faith. When grounded in biblical truth, however, therapy can be a powerful tool that complements your spiritual growth.

Both secular and Christian therapy focus on decreasing symptoms of distress, improving the ability to function in daily life, and developing coping skills for managing stress. However, secular therapy emphasizes autonomy and self-fulfillment rather than acknowledging God’s sovereignty and obeying His wisdom and authority.

Christian counseling, on the other hand, combines conventional strategies with biblical principles and insights, spiritual support, and prayer. If you would like to set up an appointment to meet with one of the faith-based counselors in our online directory, please give us a call.
